hints: Look at the nuclide symbols $^{1}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$: the lower number $Z=1$ and the upper number $A=1$ or $A=2$ tell you protons and total nucleons.
Remember nuclear charge is set by the number of protons while nuclear mass is set by the total number of protons plus neutrons.
Compare $Q/m$ for one proton of charge $+e$ with mass near $1\text{u}$ against one proton of charge $+e$ with mass near $2\text{u}$.
walkthrough: Read the symbols: for $^{A}_{Z}\text{H}$, $Z$ is proton number and $A$ is nucleon number. Both have $Z=1$, with $A=1$ for hydrogen and $A=2$ for deuterium.
Count the particles: hydrogen nucleus is $1$ proton and $0$ neutrons; deuterium nucleus is $1$ proton and $1$ neutron. A neutral atom has electrons equal to $Z$, so both atoms have $1$ electron.
State the charge rule: nuclear charge $Q = Z e$. With $Z=1$ for both, $Q = +e$ for both nuclei.
State the mass rule: nuclear mass follows $A$. So $m$ for deuterium at $A=2$ is about twice $m$ for hydrogen at $A=1$.
Form charge per unit mass $Q/m$. Same numerator $+e$ divided by about twice the denominator gives about half the value for deuterium compared with hydrogen. This is option D.

options.A: Both atoms have proton number $Z=1$, so each neutral atom has one electron. Isotopes differ in neutrons, not electrons.
options.B: Both nuclei contain one proton, so both have charge $+e$. A hydrogen nucleus is a single proton and is not neutral.
options.C: Deuterium $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ has one proton plus one neutron, so its nucleus is about twice as massive as $^{1}_{1}\text{H}$, not less massive.
options.D: Both nuclei have the same charge $+e$ but deuterium has about twice the mass, so its charge per unit mass $Q/m$ is about half that of hydrogen.
